---
title: "Computational model of aesthetics"
description: >-
  Aesthetic preferences as a policy for sampling perceptual-prior gradients.
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- Aesthetic preferences may arise from optimizing how an agent moves and directs
  attention to collect samples for learning a perceptual prior.
- The primary candidate model uses behavioral network optimization (BNO). The
  work policy determines which latents the prior should predict. The play
  policy learns where to look from work trajectories, giving more weight to
  trajectories with larger prior-loss gradient norms.
- In the glyph experiment, work draws control exposure, and liking is the
  card’s play policy logit rescaled from 0 to 1 across the deck. The experiment
  tests whether BNO can match the human ideograph liking curve across exposure
  counts and whether it learns the prior in fewer fitted card draws than a
  work-only control.
:::

## What counts as a preference?

An agent looking at a painting can return its gaze to a detail or move on.
Both choices affect what it sees next. The hypothesis is that a repeatable
preference for one choice over the other can emerge from training the policy
that collects experience for perceptual learning. The model is about choices:
it does not require a stimulus to carry a beauty score or the agent to register
how much it learned after each glance.

In the [partially observable environment](pomdp-rl.qmd), a learned
[perceptual encoder](perceptual-representations.qmd) maps input $x_t$ to a
latent $z_t$. Both policies select movement and attention using $z_t$ and a
memory $h_t$ of earlier experience. The **work policy** pursues task return.
The **play policy** learns where to look to estimate the prior’s loss gradient
under the work policy.

The [efficient encoding
account](perceptual-representations.qmd#efficient-encoding) motivates fitting a
normalized prior $R_\theta(z)$ to the encoder's outputs.
The prior is meant to fit the distribution of latents encountered under the work
policy. Sampling with the play policy changes how the prior gradient is
estimated, not which distribution the prior should fit.

## Primary candidate: behavioral network optimization

In this application of [behavioral network optimization
(BNO)](behavioral-network-optimization.qmd), the target network is the
perceptual prior.

For a realized trajectory
$\tau$ with latent sequence $z_{1:T}$, define
$$
L_\theta(\tau)=-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T\log R_\theta(z_t),\qquad
G_\theta(\tau)=\nabla_\theta L_\theta(\tau).
$$ {#eq-trajectory-loss-gradient}
The prior scores each latent without conditioning on history; the samples
need not be independent. Differentiate with respect to the **prior parameters**,
holding the trajectory fixed. Average the per-step gradient vectors before taking their
norm: two glances can each produce a large gradient yet largely cancel in the
trajectory mean.

When fitting the play policy by [weighted trajectory log-likelihood],
each work trajectory's gradient norm $\|G_\theta(\tau)\|_2$ weights the
log-likelihood of its entire action sequence. The [network
update](behavioral-network-optimization.qmd#eq-defensive-network-gradient)
combines importance-weighted work and play trajectories to estimate the prior
gradient under the work policy. The encoder and work policy are held fixed
during each prior update, so its target is the distribution of latents under
the current task behavior.

[weighted trajectory log-likelihood]:
  behavioral-network-optimization.qmd#eq-weighted-trajectory-log-likelihood

An alternative [reverse-KL model](aesthetics-reverse-kl.qmd) fits the
distribution of individual latents instead. It gives each observed latent an
intrinsic reward; neither that reward nor its density-ratio estimator is
required by BNO.

## Testing the model

With the encoder, work policy, and prior checkpoint held fixed, does sampling
with the fitted play policy alongside the work policy reduce the variance of the
prior gradient estimate relative to the same number of work trajectories alone?
A separate behavioral test is whether the play policy’s predicted gaze choices
match observed preferences. Success on the sampling test alone would not
establish the aesthetic hypothesis.

### Mere exposure: Glyphs on cards

In a meta-analysis of human studies, @montoya2017 found that liking for visual
stimuli rose with repetition and then fell. The glyph experiment tests two
hypotheses:

1. **Preference.** We can fit BNO hyperparameters so that the agent’s mean
   liking at each observed work exposure count matches the rating on the
   [human ideograph curve](#ideograph-exposure-curve) at that count.
2. **Prior convergence.** BNO will need fewer fitted card draws than the
   work-only control to reach the same mean prior-loss threshold under the
   work distribution.

**Manipulating exposure.** Each card depicts a procedurally generated glyph
with a known label. At each step the agent draws one card with replacement.
Work and play each use a distribution over the deck that does not depend on
previous draws. The experimenter fixes the work distribution, assigning cards
different draw probabilities. A card’s assigned probability controls its
expected exposure; its measured exposure is the number of times it was
actually drawn during work. Some cards have zero work probability but remain
available during play, providing the zero-exposure baseline. Because the
work distribution also determines which cards train the play policy, the
liking curve describes preference under this sampling schedule, not the
effect of repetition at a fixed work probability.

**Learning the labels and the prior.** The work task is to label each glyph
from its raw image. Each work draw supplies one example in a minibatch for a
deep visual classifier, trained by cross-entropy against the known labels.
Only the classifier learns from that objective. The prior $R_\theta$ instead
predicts the classifier’s output labels $z_t$, using the mean negative log
likelihood in @eq-trajectory-loss-gradient. BNO fits the play distribution
from work trajectories weighted by their prior-loss gradient norms, then
updates the prior from the importance-weighted mixture of work and play.

**Measuring liking.** After training, let $\ell_i$ be the play policy’s logit
for card $i$, before softmax converts logits to draw probabilities. Define
the card’s liking score by rescaling its logit across all cards in the deck:
$$
L_i=\frac{\ell_i-\min_j\ell_j}{\max_j\ell_j-\min_j\ell_j}.
$$ {#eq-glyph-liking}
The least-liked cards score 0 and the most-liked score 1. If all logits are
equal, the policy expresses no preference and the score is undefined.

**Fitting hyperparameters.** For each candidate, group cards by the number
of times they were drawn during work. At each represented count $x$, compare
the group’s mean liking score with the human rating $q(x)$ from
@eq-ideograph-rating, on its published scale. The endpoints 0 and 1 apply
to individual card scores; do not rescale the group means or the human curve.
Choose the hyperparameters that minimize the mean squared difference across
represented counts, weighting each count equally regardless of how many cards
it contains. A candidate with all logits equal has no defined error.
Report the error and plot the observed group means against the human curve
to show where the agent’s liking rises or falls with exposure.

**Measuring convergence.** Starting from the same classifier and prior
checkpoint, hold the classifier and work distribution fixed. A **fitted card
draw** is a draw in a trajectory used to estimate the prior gradient. For
BNO, count the draws in both work and play trajectories used in the
importance-weighted estimate. For the control, count the draws in work
trajectories used in its prior gradient estimate. Draws used only to fit the
play policy do not count. Give both methods the same fitted-draw budget and
record how many fitted draws each needs to reach the prior-loss threshold.

## Appendix: Ideograph exposure curve {#ideograph-exposure-curve}

For $x$ exposures, the ideograph row in Table 3 of @montoya2017 gives the
following quadratic for the fitted human rating:
$$
q(x) = 0.60776 + 0.00368x - 0.000025x^2.
$$ {#eq-ideograph-rating}

The table reports a peak at 73.07 exposures. For fitting, we use the printed
coefficients in @eq-ideograph-rating, which give a peak at
$p = 0.00368/(2 \times 0.000025) = 73.6$ exposures.
